Play a piano note and hold it: it starts with a hard knock and then fades, even while you hold the key.
Bow a violin note: it swells in gently and stays as long as the bow moves. Same pitch, same harmonics
perhaps, but they don't sound like the same instrument. The difference is the **envelope**: how the
loudness of a note changes from the moment it starts to the moment it is gone.

**How to use the page.** Press **▶ Demo**, or play the computer keys (a w s e d f t g y h u j k), the
on-screen keyboard or a MIDI keyboard. Hold some notes down and let go of others quickly: the envelope
only makes sense when you hear the difference between *pressing* and *letting go*.

## The four stages: ADSR

<div class="sk" data-w="envelope"></div>

A synth describes an envelope with four numbers, **A D S R**:

- **Attack**: how long the note takes to reach full volume after you press the key. Short for a drum or
  a pluck; long for strings swelling in.
- **Decay**: how long it then takes to fall to the sustain level.
- **Sustain**: a *level*, not a time: how loud the note stays **while you hold the key**. 100% means
  no decay at all (an organ); 0% means the note dies away even if you hold it (a piano, a guitar).
- **Release**: how long the note takes to fade to silence **after you let go**.

The strip draws the shape: rising for the attack, falling for the decay, flat while you hold, falling
after you let go. The part that is flat lasts as long as your finger is down; the other three are times.

## Hear the instruments in it

Try the presets, each on a **sine** and then a **sawtooth**:

| Preset | A | D | S | R | Like |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Organ** | instant | — | 100% | instant | an organ: on or off, nothing in between |
| **Piano** | instant | long | 0% | short | the note dies away while held, and stops when you let go |
| **Pluck** | instant | short | 0% | short | a guitar, a harp, a marimba |
| **Brass** | a little | short | 70% | short | a "blat" at the start, then a steady tone |
| **Strings** | slow | — | high | medium | bowed strings fading in and out |
| **Pad** | very slow | — | high | very long | the soft wash under a pop song |
| **Click** | 1 ms | — | 100% | 1 ms | too fast: listen to the click at each end |

**Click** shows why attack and release are never quite zero: switching a wave on or off instantly
makes a click, because a sudden jump has every frequency in it (look at the spectrum as a note starts).

Now play **fast notes** with the **Pad** preset: the notes never get loud before you let go. A long
attack and fast playing don't mix. That's why string sections can't play very fast passages loudly.

## The VCA, and envelopes on other things

In a synth the envelope drives an **amplifier** (on analog synths a **VCA**, voltage-controlled
amplifier). But an envelope is just a shape that rises and falls with each note, so it can move
anything. In [subtractive synthesis](sound-subtractive.qmd) a second envelope opens and closes the
**filter**, so a note can start bright and turn dull, which is how most synth basses and brass work.
On a drum synth an envelope bends the **pitch**: the "boom" of a kick drum is a sine wave whose pitch
drops fast.
